t: Introduction: examination of the nervous system and aim of the topic
n: In this lecture we will consider the examination of the nervous system. Findings in the central nervous system, that is, the CNS, can be decisive in forensic medicine for determining the cause of death and in court proceedings. The outline has three parts. Part one: the review by Oura and colleagues, which analysed 122 original articles from 2010–2022. Part two: the method of the Farhat group, that is, sampling from white matter lesions using 7 Tesla magnetic resonance imaging and a 3D-printed mould. Part three: the Matschke 2026 update, which considers abusive head trauma, sudden unexpected death in epilepsy and artificial intelligence.

t: Neuropathology and forensic pathology: the difference
n: First, let us distinguish two closely related disciplines. Neuropathology studies small tissue samples in detail using advanced methods, for example histology, IHC and sequencing. Forensic pathology, by contrast, determines the cause and manner of death mainly from macroscopic findings, together with an assessment of the circumstances. Its problem lies in objectivity and reproducibility. Attention: neuropathology is not the same as forensic pathology. Forensic neuropathology combines the strengths of both.

t: Why examination of the CNS matters
n: Why is examination of the central nervous system important? Neurological diseases and CNS injury are among the common causes of death worldwide. A full post-mortem examination of the CNS often requires special skill and complex tissue-processing methods. For this reason, neuropathological expertise is highly valued in clinical and forensic pathology. At the same time, studies in the forensic field are less common than in clinical neuropathology.

t: Scoping review: search and selection process
n: Now let us see how the review was conducted. The search was run in the MEDLINE database on 12 February 2022, covering the period from 1 January 2010. English-language original articles in which a neuropathological method was applied to human material were selected. Papers without a neuropathological method, dealing only with imaging, fluids, identification of persons or bone fractures, were excluded. The chain is as follows: 5053 initial results, 2864 articles in the target period, screening of titles and abstracts, full-text review where necessary, and finally 122 articles included.

Let us look at the volume of publications. Worldwide, only 3–17 articles were published per year, that is, scientific activity is relatively low. Most articles appeared in forensic medicine journals, which is 57.4 per cent, and the median impact factor of the journals was 2.3. By geography, 39.3 per cent of articles came from Europe and 36.1 per cent from Asia. Articles from American groups are few, and over the whole period only two articles came from Africa.

Now the sample characteristics. The median sample was 57 individuals, the interquartile range 29–101, and the full range 4–1222. The median lower and upper age limits were 16 and 80 years. In more than a quarter of the studies age was not recorded, more precisely in 27.0 per cent. A control group is present in 43.4 per cent of studies, that is, in fewer than half; therefore most studies are descriptive in nature. Adult-only samples account for 30.3 per cent.

Ranking of research topics. Most studies were devoted to traumatic intracranial injury: of 122 articles, 24.6 per cent were on this topic. In second place is anatomy, 12.3 per cent, in which vessels and brain weight were studied. In third place is drug addiction, 11.5 per cent. Sudden unexpected death in infants and children accounted for 6.6 per cent. Little-studied topics: suicide, asphyxia, drowning, hypothermia and hyperthermia, and estimation of the time since death. Attention: much has been written on anatomy, but its contribution to forensic neuropathology is relatively small.

We move on to the methods used. Immunotechniques, that is, immunohistochemistry and immunoblotting, were the most widely used: 31.1 per cent of studies. They determine the marker and age of injury, but the findings are preliminary and need confirmation. Macroscopy, 21.3 per cent, shows the forms of injury but is often limited to description alone. Genetic methods were used for tissue identification and analysis of gene expression. Measurement of brain weight is a crude method. Attention: a preliminary finding does not mean a validated method; many new results still require further verification.

t: Case analysis: small sample and work without a control
n: Now a case analysis. A researcher found a new marker with immunotechniques in a small sample, but there is no control group. In the source the median sample is 57 people. A control group was present in only 43.4 per cent of studies, whereas a comparative design is essential for many scientific conclusions. Even when the sample is small, a statistical power calculation is rarely reported; if the age range is wide, the group becomes heterogeneous. Question: how far can such a conclusion be trusted? Answer: it is considered preliminary and must be confirmed in a large, controlled study.

Understudied topics and future directions. Even for the most studied topic, traumatic intracranial injury, tools for estimating the age of injury are still lacking, and major advances are awaited. Anatomy studies are useful to neurosurgeons, but their contribution to forensic neuropathology is small. More research is needed to find substance-specific markers and to distinguish poisoning from other causes of death. Understudied: suicide, asphyxia, drowning, hypothermia, hyperthermia, SUDEP and estimation of the post-mortem interval.

t: Quick question 1: results of the review
n: Let us reinforce the results of the review with quick questions. First question: which topic was studied most in the 122 original articles from 2010–2022? Second question: which method was used most often and in what share of articles was it used? Hint: worldwide only 3–17 articles were published per year, that is, there is little research in this field. Attention, risk of error: anatomy, 12.3%, is second, substance abuse, 11.5%, is third; not first.

We move to part two: white matter lesions. On magnetic resonance imaging, that is, MRI, they are among the most common features of ageing. An increasing lesion burden is strongly associated with the risk of stroke, cognitive decline, dementia and death. On a T2-weighted image the lesion is hyperintense, that is, bright; on a T1-weighted image it is hypointense, that is, dark. Possible causes: demyelination, axonal damage, gliosis. At the histological level, lesions are still insufficiently studied, so MRI must be linked with histology.

The general scheme of MRI-guided sampling is as follows. Placing the left hemisphere in an agar-sucrose medium protects the tissue from movement and deformation. It is then scanned on a 7 Tesla MRI and sliced with a 3D guide. The surface of each cut slab is photographed, which is called a blockface, and registered to the MRI slices. A deep learning model finds the lesion on T1; the neuropathologist takes a sample from the lesion according to the mask.

Why is the agar-sucrose medium needed? It reduces motion artefact and protects the brain from deformation during cutting. In 7 T magnetic resonance imaging, the dielectric properties of the medium should be close to those of the brain. Water and ordinary agar have a relative permittivity of about 78, brain tissue about 58. If sucrose is added to the agar, the relative permittivity falls from 78 to 68 and approaches that of the brain.

t: Steps of embedding the brain in agar
n: Steps of embedding the brain in agar. First a solution of 1.5% agar and 30% sucrose is prepared, heated at 65–68°C for 2–3 hours and cooled to 42°C. The brain is taken out of 10% formalin, and the warm solution is slowly poured onto the gyri with a pipette. The ventricles are filled first, then the solution is poured around with massage so that bubbles escape. The brain is held submerged for 2–3 minutes so that the agar, as it thickens, does not let it float up. It then sets for 2–3 hours and the lid is closed.

The 3D-printed container and cutting guide consist of four parts. The body protects the brain from deformation; the wall and base are 3 mm. The guide holds the blade in the coronal plane; it has 28 upper and 29 lower pillars. The pillars are 4 mm in diameter with a gap of 0.6 mm. The pillars are arranged along a belt; a blade 0.5 mm thick is passed between them. The lid closes the body: after closing, agar is added through the inlet opening and air is drawn out through the outlet opening. All three parts are printed on a 3D printer; one set is enough for about 30 brains.

7T MRI sequences. Three sequences were used. GRE: voxel 0.37 × 0.37 × 0.37 mm, time 36 minutes 59 seconds. T2-SPACE: voxel 0.41 × 0.41 × 0.41 mm, time 46 minutes 19 seconds. T1w MP2RAGE: voxel 0.37 × 0.37 × 0.37 mm, time 32 minutes 28 seconds. On T2-SPACE images the pillars appear black; registration was performed in exactly this sequence. On the T1w MP2RAGE image, the deep learning model automatically delineated white matter changes.

Steps of guided cutting of the brain. First the lid is removed, the medium is drained along the wall, and the guide is lifted out, held by the square pillars. Then the coronal cut is made between the pillars. The blade is 0.5 mm; at each cut two pairs of pillars are skipped. Then the blade marks are photographed. Parts not covered by the pillars are cut by hand; the pieces are stored for up to one week in 10% formalin.

t: Registration of MRI and blockface images
n: Registration of MRI and blockface images. The pillars appear white on the blockface and black on T2-SPACE, and serve as reliable markers, that is, fiducials. It was assumed that the blade travelled along a coronal virtual plane between a pair of pillars. In the RadiAnt viewer the plane is matched to the blade mark. The match is confirmed visually, that is, qualitatively, and then one moves on to the next slice. Finally, the mask is transferred to the blockface.

Lesion segmentation and sampling are carried out in four steps. First, MRI: white matter lesions are visible on magnetic resonance imaging in the T1 and T2 sequences and guide the sampling. Second, segmentation: the authors' own deep learning model automatically identified lesions on the T1 image. Third, the mask: the lesion mask was transferred from the MRI to the blockface photograph. The blockface is a photograph of the surface of the cut piece. Fourth, the sample: using the mask and the saved registration, the neuropathologist took a histological sample from the exact place on the physical slab.

The results were tested on two brains. In both brains there were 18 coronal slabs in total; of these 14 were cut with the guide and 4 by hand. Registration of the 14 guided slabs took about 30 minutes per brain. The four hand-cut slabs took longer: about one hour each. In the first brain the lesions were periventricular, with 2 deep foci; in the second brain periventricular. In both brains the lesions in the periventricular region extended from front to back.

t: Limitations of the review and study design
n: Let us look at the limitations of the review and the study design. Although the sample size is moderate, a statistical power calculation is rarely reported. More than half of the studies have no control group; most studies are descriptive, whereas a comparative design is needed for a scientific conclusion. The age range is wide: generalisation is good, but if the sample is small the group becomes heterogeneous; in a quarter of studies the youngest and oldest ages are not recorded. Limitations of the review: articles with unusual terminology may have been missed; only original articles were taken; formal risk of bias was not assessed.

t: Advantages and limitations of the method
n: Advantages and limitations of the method. Advantages: the kit is reusable and inexpensive, about 60 dollars, sufficient for about 30 brains, that is, about 2 dollars per brain. It suits different brain sizes, and the slabs are reproducible and uniform. Limitations: one kit takes about 42 hours to print, the guide does not cover the whole brain, and the orientation must be planned before setting. Bubbles produce artefact on gradient-echo, that is, GRE, images near the sulci and hippocampus. Registration was assessed visually; quantitative measures could be added in future.

Let us remember the typical mistakes. Attention: white matter foci are hyperintense, bright, on T2 and hypointense, dark, on T1. Do not confuse the two. Also: guided cutting is not the same as hand cutting. Areas beyond the reach of the guide are cut by hand, but parallel to the slices. In both brains, of the 18 coronal slabs, 14 were cut with the guide and 4 by hand; registration of the hand-cut ones takes considerably longer, about 1 hour. Remember the order: Agar, MRI, Cutting, Registration, Sampling. The initial letters: A-M-C-R-S.

t: Case analysis: agar with bubbles and artefact
n: Case analysis: agar with bubbles and artefact. Situation: air bubbles remaining in the agar produced artefact on the GRE image near the sulci and hippocampus. Question: what is the cause and how is it reduced? Cause: air bubbles remaining in the agar produce a magnetic susceptibility artefact. This mainly affects GRE images. Reduction: air is drawn out through the inlet and outlet ports in the lid, and agar is added. The ventricle is filled first, and massage is applied during pouring. Limitation: despite refinement of the method, completely eliminating bubbles is still difficult.

A quick question on the MRI method. First: approximately how thick is a coronal slab in mm? Answer: about 9.8 mm; the guide ensures uniform cutting. Second: what serves as the fiducial marker? Answer: the pillars of the guide; they appear white on the blockface photograph and black on the T2-SPACE image. Third: why is sucrose added? Answer: the relative dielectric permittivity of the agar falls from 78 to 68, approaching the brain value of about 58. Fourth: what is the image resolution? Answer: 370 µm isotropic resolution at 7 Tesla.

Part three, the update. In post-mortem radiology, PMCT, that is, post-mortem computed tomography, documents injury non-invasively. PMMR, that is, post-mortem magnetic resonance imaging, was first described in 1990. ESPR, that is, the European Society of Paediatric Radiology, updated its protocols in 2021 and 2025. Early versions stretched to 90 minutes, which is too long for everyday work. ESPR 2021: 30–60 minutes. Minimal protocol 2025: under 30 minutes, 3-D T2 and T1, brain and body. Ideal protocol: more time, whole body 3-D, SWI and DWI.

t: Estimating time of death with CSF biomarkers
n: Estimating time of death with cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers. PMI, that is, the post-mortem interval, is imprecise by classical signs, so cerebrospinal fluid and vitreous humour are analysed. Cecchi and colleagues studied 35 people: mean PMI 2.94 days, range 1–6 days. GFAP rises up to day 3, then declines slightly. S100B rises with PMI up to day 5. NSE changes erratically. GFAP, S100B and NSE are especially promising in the first 2 days; more observation is necessary.

t: Case analysis: determining the time of death
n: Case analysis: determining the time of death. Situation: a body is found, time of death unknown; temperature, rigor mortis and livor mortis are imprecise under the influence of environmental and individual factors. Approach: GFAP and S100B are measured in the cerebrospinal fluid. GFAP rises up to about 3 days, while S100B rises up to day 5. Limitation: the basis is a study of 35 people, without nervous system pathology, mean PMI 2.94 days; the change in NSE was erratic. Question: how reliable is this method? The author calls it especially promising in the first 2 days, but studies with more people are needed.

t: Abusive head trauma in children: biomechanics
n: Abusive head trauma in children, that is, AHT, from the biomechanical point of view. AHT is a syndrome of injuries in an infant caused by impact or violent shaking. Models: 2 animal, 5 physical and 10 mathematical studies. Injury thresholds were taken from adults or animals. Sagittal angular acceleration is considered the main mechanism; AHT most often occurs at 2–4 months of age. With a gyroscope and accelerometer: in a 6-week-old manikin, head and body acceleration is higher and better matches injury kinematics; in a 1-year-old manikin it is lower and matches less well.

AHT: encephalopathy and neuroradiology. Main findings: hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, traumatic axonal injury, and subdural and retinal haemorrhage. Hypothesis: focal traumatic axonal injury in the lower brainstem near the cardiorespiratory nuclei leads to respiratory arrest; this has not yet been fully proven. In the Hahnemann study, 31 of 61 children, that is, 50.8 per cent, had a lesion; no brainstem lesion was found, and most survived. Attention: not being seen on neuroradiology does not mean absence on pathology. Small lesions may not be visible; clinicopathological correlation is needed.

t: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy and domestic violence
n: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy and domestic violence. The effect of repeated traumatic brain injury was called “punch drunk” nearly a century ago; now it is CTE. The work of Omalu raised interest. In the 1990 female case, whether it was CTE remained unclear. The first definite case of CTE in a young woman, a victim of intimate partner violence, was reported in 2021. In 14 women with a history of intimate partner violence, CTE was not found; the reason may be the composition of the sample. Quantifying the number and force of blows is almost impossible. In the LETBI project, 7 of 47 donor brains, that is, 14.9 per cent, had definite CTE; a single TBI was weakly associated with CTE.

SUDEP: a diagnosis of exclusion. SUDEP is sudden unexpected death in epilepsy; the diagnosis is made after other causes have been excluded. In a follow-up of more than 2500 patients, 38 people, that is, 1.54%, died of SUDEP: 4.76 per 1000 person-years. Sleep and the prone position are common features. Variants of sodium channel genes are more frequent, and subtle anomalies have been found in the hippocampus. Risk factors: living alone, prolonged apnoea. Attention: SUDEP is not the same as status epilepticus; both are direct causes of death in epilepsy.

Artificial intelligence in forensic neuropathology. The systematic review by Treglia and co-authors found 34 papers between 2014 and May 2024: on TBI and epilepsy. On TBI there were only 6 papers, all radiological: a CNN on PMCT distinguished head injury that led to death. On epilepsy and tumours there were 28 papers: AI classified tumours with high accuracy and distinguished focal cortical dysplasia from tuberous sclerosis with >90% accuracy. AI can provide objective, reproducible evidence, but the introduction of complex methods into everyday practice is unlikely for now.

Cerebellum, brain morphology and alcohol. The cerebellum may act as a “witness box”: it may show valproate or alcohol toxicity, that is, atrophy of the superior vermis and thiamine deficiency, as well as herniation. Supratentorial TBI, even without direct cerebellar damage, may cause atrophy years later, especially in children. In imaging of 17 focal lesions associated with criminal behaviour, disruption of the right uncinate fasciculus was found, but the image alone does not prove causation. Alcohol-related brain damage impairs working memory and attention; recent work has shown microglial change rather than neuronal loss.

t: Case analysis: SUDEP and the autopsy finding
n: Case analysis: SUDEP and the autopsy finding. Situation: a person with epilepsy is found dead. The autopsy reveals no other cause of death. Question: what conclusion will the neuropathologist reach? SUDEP is the sudden, unexpected, non-accidental death of a person with epilepsy. If no other cause is found at autopsy, this diagnosis is made; it is a diagnosis of exclusion. The neuropathologist's main task is to exclude other causes of death. He or she may also find a previously unknown epileptogenic condition. Attention, risk of error: SUDEP is not status epilepticus. Both are direct causes of death, but SUDEP is diagnosed when no other cause is found.

A quick question on new directions. First question, AHT: with which kinematic parameter is the main mechanism producing typical injuries in infants linked? Second question, SUDEP: what type of diagnosis is this, and name three factors that raise the risk? Third question, cerebrospinal fluid: which three biomarkers were studied in the cerebrospinal fluid for estimating the time of death? Fourth question, PMMR: how long does the minimal protocol of post-mortem MRI take, and what does it cover?

t: Conclusion: features of the forensic neuropathology technique
n: Conclusion. The field is changing from a descriptive science to an integrative one: macroscopic findings are interpreted together with biomechanics, neuroradiology, genetics and bioinformatics. Linking MRI and histology: 7 Tesla MRI, a 3D-printed guide and MRI–blockface registration allow targeted sampling from white matter foci. Limitation: 3–17 articles were published per year, samples averaged 57 people, and a control group is present in 43.4% of studies. Many findings are preliminary and require confirmation. Next steps: collaboration of forensic pathologist, neuroradiologist and bioengineers, adequate sample size, control groups, prospective clinicopathological correlation.
